nodes.label: Quest start
nodes.blurb: Runs once when the quest begins. Setup goes here.

fields.text: Each lifecycle node is an independent starting point — they never connect to each other. Wire the chain that should run when this moment happens. Event listeners belong under “On start & reload”; anything wired to “Quest start” is wiped when the player reloads.

nodes.label: On start & reload
nodes.blurb: Runs on claim and every load. Listeners go here.

fields.text: Each lifecycle node is an independent starting point — they never connect to each other. Wire the chain that should run when this moment happens. Event listeners belong under “On start & reload”; anything wired to “Quest start” is wiped when the player reloads.

nodes.label: On quest complete
nodes.blurb: Runs after a Complete quest node, auto-complete, or Complete button finishes the quest.

fields.text: Each lifecycle node is an independent starting point — they never connect to each other. Wire the chain that should run when this moment happens. Event listeners belong under “On start & reload”; anything wired to “Quest start” is wiped when the player reloads.

nodes.label: On quest abandoned
nodes.blurb: Runs if the player gives up. Cleanup goes here.

fields.text: Each lifecycle node is an independent starting point — they never connect to each other. Wire the chain that should run when this moment happens. Event listeners belong under “On start & reload”; anything wired to “Quest start” is wiped when the player reloads.

nodes.label: Objective
nodes.blurb: A task the player must complete

fields.label: Identifier
fields.hint: A short unique name for this objective so other nodes can refer to it. Lowercase with dashes reads well.

fields.label: Shown to the player
fields.hint: The line shown in the player's quest journal. A clear instruction tends to read well, but any wording that fits your quest works.

fields.label: Hint
fields.hint: Revealed only if the player asks for help. As gentle or as cryptic as you want it to be.

fields.label: Extra info
fields.hint: Extra detail in the journal's expanded view. Good for lore or background.

fields.label: Suggested command
fields.hint: Suggested command shown in the journal. It runs nothing — it is a copy-pasteable nudge.

fields.label: Hidden until unlocked
fields.hint: Keep the objective out of the journal until another objective unlocks it. Use for twists.

nodes.label: When event
nodes.blurb: React to something the player does

fields.label: Game event
fields.hint: All supported HackHub events, listed with the details each one carries.

fields.label: Only when
fields.hint: Leave empty to fire on any occurrence.

nodes.label: Create network
nodes.blurb: Routers, devices, firewalls and ports

fields.label: Devices
fields.hint: The router at the root of the network, plus everything behind it. Routers and splitters carry children; firewalls carry rules.

fields.label: Also remove this network when the quest is completed
fields.hint: Off by default: the network stays in the world after the quest, the way a real company would. It is also safer, because deleting a machine the player is still connected to can hang the game. Abandoning the quest removes it either way.

nodes.label: Create Wi-Fi
nodes.blurb: A crackable access point

fields.text: Game note: Bettercap may show no network name after you pick a mod-created access point by BSSID. Scanning, joining and cracking still worked in QA; use the BSSID as the fixed clue.

fields.label: Network name (SSID)
fields.hint: The network name shown in the in-game Wi-Fi list.

fields.label: WPA passphrase
fields.hint: The passphrase the player must discover. Make sure some node in your quest reveals it.

fields.label: Signal strength
fields.hint: The game's Wi-Fi scale: 0 = weakest, 3 = strongest. It also drives how long joining takes.

fields.label: BSSID
fields.hint: Optional MAC address shown for the access point. Leave blank to let the game pick one.

fields.label: Channel
fields.hint: Optional 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz channel shown by scans. Leave blank to let the game pick one for the SSID's band.

fields.label: Advertises WPS
fields.hint: Whether Wi-Fi scans show WPS for this access point. Leave off unless your story needs to pin it.

fields.label: Router model
fields.hint: Enables the in-game `fern` recovery route. Leave blank to disable it.

fields.label: Router accounts
fields.hint: Accounts on the access point's own system. Their files land in /home/<username>/.

fields.label: Username
fields.hint: The login name for ssh, ftp or a web login page.

fields.label: Password
fields.hint: Leave blank to let the game pick one.

fields.label: First name
fields.hint: Shown on the account's profile page and in whois results.

fields.label: Last name
fields.hint: Shown on the account's profile page and in whois results.

fields.label: E-mail
fields.hint: The account's e-mail address. Useful as a lead the player can mail.

fields.label: Accepts reverse TCP
fields.hint: Lets the player open a connection from this account back to their own machine. Turn on only if your quest needs it.

fields.label: Router ports
fields.hint: Open ports on the access point itself.

fields.label: External port
fields.hint: The port number as seen from outside. This is what nmap reports and what the player connects to.

fields.label: Internal port
fields.hint: The port the service actually listens on inside the machine. Leave equal to the external port unless you are deliberately redirecting.

fields.label: Service
fields.hint: What nmap prints next to the port, e.g. http, ssh, ftp, mysql. Free text — it is a label, not a real service.

fields.label: Version
fields.hint: The banner nmap -sV prints. Use three numbers and no letters — metasploit refuses "7.2" and "7.2p2", leaving the player unable to run the exploit. Blank omits the version line.

fields.label: Open
fields.hint: Closed ports show as filtered to nmap.

fields.label: Devices behind the access point
fields.hint: Machines reachable through this access point. Add a router here to build a second network hop.

fields.label: Also remove this access point when the quest is completed
fields.hint: Off by default: the access point stays in the world after the quest. Abandoning the quest removes it either way.

nodes.label: Firewall rule
nodes.blurb: Allow or block a port

fields.label: Protected IP
fields.hint: The machine these rules protect: the quest's own network, or one machine you name.

options.label: Random — the quest's network
options.meaning: the address the game gave your network

fields.label: Port
fields.hint: The port this rule applies to.

fields.label: Allowed
fields.hint: Off means the port is blocked by the firewall.

fields.label: Source
fields.hint: Which machines the rule applies to: anywhere on the internet, or one machine you name.

options.label: Anywhere
options.meaning: matches every machine on the internet

fields.label: Destination
fields.hint: The machine the rule protects — usually the one in “Protected IP” above. Picking it copies that address; changing it later won't follow.

fields.label: Locked
fields.hint: The player cannot remove a locked rule.

fields.label: Remove when the quest ends
fields.hint: Drop the firewall when the quest ends so the machine is reachable afterwards.

nodes.label: Change port
nodes.blurb: Open, close, add or remove a port

fields.text: Adjusts a machine that already exists — one your “Create network” node built. To add the machine itself, use “Create network”; to open, close, add or remove one of its ports later in the story, use this.

fields.label: Device IP
fields.hint: A router IP or any device behind it.

fields.label: Action
fields.hint: Open makes an existing port reachable. Close blocks it. Add creates a new service; Remove deletes it entirely.

options.label: Close
options.hint: Closing internal port 22 also drops live SSH sessions.

fields.label: External port
fields.hint: The port number as seen from outside — what nmap reports.

fields.label: Internal port
fields.hint: The port the service listens on inside the machine.

fields.label: Service
fields.hint: What nmap prints next to the port, e.g. http, ssh, mysql.

fields.label: Open
fields.hint: Turn off to make the port appear closed.

fields.label: Restore when the quest ends
fields.hint: Put the port back the way it was when the quest ends.

nodes.label: Register domain
nodes.blurb: Point a hostname at an IP

fields.label: Domain
fields.hint: The hostname the player types, e.g. vault.corp-internal.net.

fields.label: Resolves to
fields.hint: The address it resolves to. nslookup and dig will report this.

fields.label: Vulnerabilities
fields.hint: Weaknesses on the host behind this name. In-game scanners report them when the player probes it.

fields.label: Type
fields.hint: The kind of weakness this machine has. The in-game scanners report it when the player probes the machine.

options.label: RFI (load a file from your URL)

fields.label: Version
fields.hint: The affected component's version, e.g. "WordPress 5.8". Cosmetic unless a trigger matches on it.

fields.label: Remove when the quest ends
fields.hint: Drop the DNS entry when the quest ends.

nodes.label: Create database
nodes.blurb: Content for sqlmap and DatabaseManager

fields.label: Host IP
fields.hint: The address the player points a database client at.

fields.label: Username
fields.hint: The login sqlmap or a client uses.

fields.label: Password
fields.hint: The password. Give the player a way to find it — a config file, a leaked dump, a cracked hash.

fields.label: Tables
fields.hint: The data inside: tables holding rows of named values, ready for the player's SQL.

fields.label: Remove when the quest ends
fields.hint: Drop the database when the quest ends.

nodes.label: Place files
nodes.blurb: Drop files on a PC or a remote device

fields.label: Where
fields.hint: Whose filesystem to write to. The player's own machine is written when the flow reaches this node; a remote device is mounted with the machine, under the account the player lands in, so the files are already there when they break in.

fields.label: Device IP
fields.hint: Only used for a remote device. Use the same {{data.targetIp}} token you gave the network, and the files are mounted on that machine before the player ever connects.

fields.label: Parent folder
fields.hint: Where the files are mounted. Folders named etc, home, logs or lib are merged into the existing ones rather than replacing them.

fields.label: Files
fields.hint: The files and folders to create. A folder named etc, home, logs or lib merges with the machine's existing one.

fields.label: Name
fields.hint: The file or folder name, exactly as it appears in ls.

fields.label: Extension
fields.hint: The extension, e.g. txt, log, conf. Leave blank for folders.

fields.label: Folder
fields.hint: Mark this entry as a directory rather than a file.

fields.label: Hidden
fields.hint: Prefix the name with a dot so a plain ls does not show it.

fields.label: Contents
fields.hint: The file's contents. This is where clues live — a config file, a log excerpt, a leaked password.

nodes.label: Give data to an addon
nodes.blurb: Pick a data shape from an addon and fill it in

nodes.label: Addon node
nodes.blurb: A story node from an addon — find it under Editor Mods

nodes.label: Tool response
nodes.blurb: Script what a recon tool reports

fields.label: Tool
fields.hint: Pick the in-game command this overrides, like nmap or whois. When the player runs it on your input, they see your text instead of the usual result.

fields.label: Keyed by
fields.hint: What the player types after the command — the IP, domain or name it answers for. The tool only responds to this exact input. hydra/ssh/ftp use the user + target fields below instead.

fields.label: User
fields.hint: Only match when the player ran the command against this user.

fields.label: Target
fields.hint: Only match when the player ran the command against this host.

fields.label: Response
fields.hint: One “Label: value” per line. The editor turns them into exactly what that tool shows in-game — add a line for each thing you want the player to see.

fields.text: What each tool reads: whois → domain, ip, registrant, email · lynx → web, email, phone, social, address (anything else is shown as extra detail) · geoip → country, city, latitude, longitude · hydra → username, password · nslookup / mxlookup → ip. nmap is different: write one port per line, like “22 open ssh OpenSSH 8.9.0” — always three numbers. Tags work here too: {{data.targetIp}} is the address the game gave your network, {{data.name}} anything you saved with “Set quest data”, {{player.username}} the player's login, and {{random.password}} a fresh password.

fields.label: Remove when the quest ends
fields.hint: Stop intercepting the command when the quest ends.

nodes.label: Dialogue
nodes.blurb: A conversation with the player — phone call, Kisscord, e-mail or WeeChat

nodes.label: Twotter
nodes.blurb: Post tweets from one of the mod's Twotter accounts — one, or a profile's worth of history

fields.label: Account
fields.hint: Which of the mod's Twotter accounts posts these. Accounts are shared by every quest, so one character can carry a story arc across several of them — make one with “Manage accounts”.

fields.text: Tweets are written oldest first, the order they happened. A profile shows them the other way up — the newest at the top — and that is done by the game, not by you.

This node came from an older draft whose tweet time could not be carried over exactly — either it pinned a calendar date, or that was the draft's default. A fixed date cannot be turned into an age without reading today's clock, which the editor never does before export, so the node now says “1 month earlier”. Set the amount and unit below to the age you meant.

fields.label: Tweets
fields.hint: One row is a single post. A handful of rows with “Already on the profile” times is a history the player finds when they look the character up — a month of excitement before a disappearance, say.

fields.label: Tweet
fields.hint: What the character wrote. Tags work here, like everywhere else an author writes text.

fields.label: When
fields.hint: “When the story arrives” posts the tweet as the flow reaches this node. “Already on the profile” has it sitting there from the start, that far back.

options.label: When the story arrives
options.hint: The player sees it appear, reading “a few seconds ago”.

options.label: Already on the profile
options.hint: Backdated by the amount beside this: the profile reads “a month ago” the moment the player finds it.

fields.label: How long ago
fields.hint: Counted back from the moment the story reaches this node, on the in-game clock.

fields.label: Unit
fields.hint: Minutes through years, the same units a Timer takes.

fields.label: Likes
fields.hint: Cosmetic, but it sells the fiction. A brand-new account with 400 likes reads as fake.

fields.label: Replies
fields.hint: How many replies the post shows. The game does not open them — this is the number under the post, nothing more.

fields.label: Reposts
fields.hint: How many times the post was shared. Zero is fine and often truest — a small account screaming into the void.

fields.label: Views
fields.hint: How many people saw it. It has to look plausible next to the likes: thousands of views with two likes reads wrong.

fields.label: Also in the main timeline
fields.hint: Off keeps a year of history on the profile where the player looked for it. On drops it into the public feed too — good for an announcement the whole city should see.

nodes.label: Manual input
nodes.blurb: The player types a passphrase

fields.text: This makes a new command the player can type in the terminal. Wire the green “Correct” socket for a right answer and the red “Wrong” socket for a wrong one.

fields.label: Command name
fields.hint: The terminal command the player runs, e.g. decrypt. It appears in help output.

fields.label: Help text
fields.hint: The one-line description shown next to the command in help.

fields.label: Prompt
fields.hint: The text printed before the cursor, e.g. "Passphrase >".

fields.label: Mask the input
fields.hint: Hides typing behind * — the player sees “Passphrase > ****” instead of their answer, like a password box. Use it when the answer is a secret.

fields.label: Match
fields.hint: Exactly equals checks the whole answer. Contains accepts it anywhere in what the player types. Matches pattern is for advanced authors who want to accept a whole family of answers at once.

fields.label: Expected answer
fields.hint: The answer that counts as correct — or the pattern, if you chose “Matches pattern” above.

fields.label: Case sensitive
fields.hint: Turn off to accept any capitalisation. Recommended unless case is part of the puzzle.

fields.label: Success message
fields.hint: Printed on a match, then the green “Correct” socket fires.

fields.label: Failure message
fields.hint: Printed on a miss, then the red “Wrong” socket fires. The player can run the command again.

nodes.label: Pay the player
nodes.blurb: Deposit money

fields.label: Amount
fields.hint: Credits deposited into the player's bank account.

fields.label: Description
fields.hint: The label on the bank statement line.

fields.label: From IBAN
fields.hint: The sending account, shown in the transfer details.

fields.label: From name
fields.hint: The sender's name on the statement.

fields.text: Kept from an earlier version: this pays a percentage of the player's balance. It still works.

nodes.label: Charge the player
nodes.blurb: Withdraw money

fields.label: Amount type
fields.hint: A fixed sum, or a slice of whatever the player currently has in the bank.

fields.label: Amount
fields.hint: Credits taken from the player's account.

fields.label: Percent
fields.hint: Percentage of the player's current balance, taken when this node runs.

fields.label: Description
fields.hint: The label on the bank statement line.

nodes.label: Notify
nodes.blurb: A popup or toast

fields.label: Message
fields.hint: The text on the popup. Type {{data.name}} to insert a value you saved earlier.

fields.label: Style
fields.hint: A notification is a persistent popup; a toast slides in and fades on its own.

fields.label: Tone
fields.hint: Sets the colour and icon: info, success, warning or error.

nodes.label: Ask player
nodes.blurb: Ask for one line of text

fields.text: Shows one question when the story reaches this node. The top output fires when the player submits text; Cancelled fires when they close it without answering.

fields.label: Title
fields.hint: The heading at the top of the question box. Leave blank if the question itself is enough.

fields.label: Question
fields.hint: The sentence above the answer box — what you want the player to answer.

fields.label: Example text
fields.hint: Grey hint inside an empty answer box. It disappears as soon as the player types.

fields.label: Starts filled with
fields.hint: Text already in the answer box when it opens. Leave blank when the player should type from scratch.

fields.label: Mask typing
fields.hint: Hides what the player types, like a password box. Use for passphrases, keys and private codes.

fields.label: Save answer as
fields.hint: Optional name for the answer. If you type playerAnswer here, later nodes can read it with {{data.playerAnswer}}. Leave blank if only this choice matters.

fields.label: Accept
fields.hint: Choose whether any submitted text continues, or whether the answer must match something you set.

fields.label: Answer to accept
fields.hint: The text that counts as the right answer. Tags are filled before the check, so a saved password can be accepted too.

fields.label: Case sensitive
fields.hint: Turn off to accept any capitalisation. Turn on only when upper and lower case are part of the puzzle.

fields.text: Pattern matching is powerful but easy to make unfair. Prefer exact or contains unless several different answers should count.

nodes.label: Set quest data
nodes.blurb: Store a value for later

fields.label: Key
fields.hint: A name you choose, like doorCode. Use the same name later to read this value back.

fields.label: Value
fields.hint: Any text is fine — a word, a number, an address. It is just stored, so nothing here can error. You can also insert a live value by typing {{data.name}} for something you saved earlier.

nodes.label: Claim another quest
nodes.blurb: Chain into the next quest

fields.label: Quest
fields.hint: The identifier of the quest to start next. It must exist in this mod or another installed one.

nodes.label: Complete quest
nodes.blurb: Finish the current quest and run On quest complete

fields.text: This is a terminal ending. Put closing mail, payments and notifications before it, or place them under On quest complete.

nodes.label: Retire quest
nodes.blurb: Remove the current quest without marking it complete

fields.text: This is a terminal ending. The quest disappears without rewards and without On quest complete.

nodes.label: Unclaim quest
nodes.blurb: Remove a claimed quest from the player's list

fields.label: Quest
fields.hint: The identifier of the claimed quest to remove. Leave blank to remove this quest.

nodes.label: Run terminal command
nodes.blurb: Execute in the terminal

fields.text: Runs a command the moment the story reaches this node, as if the player had typed it — for things the story should do that the player hasn't. Example: “nmap {{data.targetIp}}” runs a scan the player can read.

fields.label: Command
fields.hint: The command executed in the player's terminal, as if they had typed it. Tags like {{data.targetIp}} are filled in first.

nodes.label: Open handbook
nodes.blurb: Jump to an in-game article

fields.label: Article
fields.hint: The page to open. In game 1.3.1 this opens the handbook on its own landing page: reaching a particular page is not possible until the page names the game uses are known (see the manual).

fields.label: Category
fields.hint: The handbook section the article sits under.

nodes.label: Branch
nodes.blurb: Split on a condition

fields.label: Test against
fields.hint: Test against details from the event that fired, or against quest data you stored earlier with a “Set quest data” node.

fields.label: Take the “Yes” path when
fields.hint: All clauses must hold for the “Yes” path. Otherwise the “No” path runs.

nodes.label: Wait
nodes.blurb: Pause before continuing

fields.label: Seconds
fields.hint: How long the story pauses here. Fractions are fine — 0.5 waits half a second.

nodes.label: Timer
nodes.blurb: Do something at a later in-game time

fields.text: Fires the next node at a later in-game time. Wait holds the story for an exact stretch — any mix of years, months, weeks, days, hours and minutes; A coming day counts calendar time from now and rings at a clock time — “in 1 month 2 weeks 2 days, at 18:23” — so it stays right however long the player leaves the quest; An exact date pins a moment in the story's own calendar. A time that has already passed fires as soon as the story reaches the node.

fields.label: When it fires
fields.hint: A stretch to wait, a clock time counted from now, or a fixed moment in the story's own calendar.

fields.label: Years
fields.hint: Whole in-game years to wait, before the shorter units beside it. A target month with fewer days uses its last day.

fields.label: Months
fields.hint: Whole in-game months to wait, on top of the years. 31 January plus one month lands on 28 February, not in March.

fields.label: Weeks
fields.hint: In-game weeks to wait, on top of the months. One week is seven in-game days.

fields.label: Days
fields.hint: In-game days to wait first. 0 is fine — the units are added up.

fields.label: Hours
fields.hint: In-game hours, on top of the days. 25 hours is a legal value.

fields.label: Minutes
fields.hint: In-game minutes, on top of the days and hours. At the default game speed one in-game minute passes every real second.

fields.label: Years
fields.hint: In-game years from now, counted from the day the story reaches this node. A target month with fewer days uses its last day.

fields.label: Months
fields.hint: In-game months from now, on top of the years. 31 January plus one month lands on 28 February, not in March.

fields.label: Weeks
fields.hint: In-game weeks from now, on top of the months. One week is seven in-game days.

fields.label: Days
fields.hint: In-game days from now, on top of the weeks and months. 0 means today, so “0 days, at 09:00” fires the next time the clock reads 09:00.

fields.label: Day
fields.hint: The in-game day of the month, as the in-game clock shows it. The field warns when that day does not exist.

fields.label: Month
fields.hint: The in-game month, by name, as the in-game clock shows it.

fields.label: Year
fields.hint: The in-game year, e.g. 2026. Read it off the in-game clock, not your own calendar.

fields.label: Hour
fields.hint: The hour the in-game clock will show, 0–23. This is the player's clock, not the wall clock.

fields.label: Minute
fields.hint: The minute the in-game clock will show, 0–59.

nodes.label: Reroute
nodes.blurb: Split or tidy a wire

fields.text: A tidy point for your wires: run a connection through here to fan it out to several nodes or to route it around clutter. It has no effect on the story itself. Tip: double-click any wire on the canvas to drop one in automatically.

nodes.label: Group frame
nodes.blurb: A named box that moves its nodes

fields.text: Draw a box around part of your quest to keep it tidy. Drag the frame and everything inside moves with it. It has no effect on how the mod runs.

fields.label: Name
fields.hint: Shown in the frame's title bar — name the cluster after what it does, e.g. “Act 1: recon”.

fields.label: Title bar colour
fields.hint: Colour-code your frames however you like — e.g. one colour per act, or per character. It only changes how the frame looks in the editor.

fields.label: Comment
fields.hint: A note to future-you about what this cluster does.

nodes.label: Random pick
nodes.blurb: Choose one option at random

fields.label: Options
fields.hint: One of these is picked at random and stored. Add as many as you like.

fields.label: Value
fields.hint: The value stored if this option is picked.

fields.label: Store the result as
fields.hint: A name you choose. The picked value is saved under it so you can read it back later with {{data.name}}.

nodes.label: Sequence
nodes.blurb: Fire several outputs one after another

fields.text: One input, as many outputs as you like. When the story reaches this node the outputs fire from top to bottom, waiting the pause you set before each one. Add or remove outputs below — each row is a socket on the node.

fields.label: Outputs, in order
fields.hint: They fire top to bottom. Drag the rows' ✕ to remove an output — any wire attached to it is removed too.

fields.label: Name
fields.hint: Free text — whatever helps you recognise this output on the canvas, e.g. “lights out” or “call Mara”.

fields.label: Wait before firing (milliseconds)
fields.hint: How long to pause before this output fires, counted from the previous one. 0 fires it immediately; 1000 is one second.

nodes.label: Debug probe
nodes.blurb: Print what is happening here

fields.label: Label
fields.hint: Names itself after whatever you wire it to — socket, node and detail. Type your own to override it.

fields.label: Include saved values
fields.hint: Print everything the quest has saved with a “Remember a value” node.

fields.label: Include the event
fields.hint: Also print the details the game passed to this point, so you can see the real values instead of guessing what arrived.

fields.label: Show on screen too
fields.hint: Also show it on screen, so you can test without reading the log file.

nodes.label: Sticky note
nodes.blurb: A comment on the canvas

fields.label: Note
fields.hint: Shown on the canvas only. Notes are never exported into the mod.

fields.label: Width
fields.hint: How wide the note is on the canvas, in pixels.

nodes.label: Story Beat
nodes.blurb: Plan a story beat — colour it, preview it

fields.text: Planning only. This node is stripped from the exported mod and never runs. Wire it among reroute, branch and sequence to sketch a flow; the story passes through it unchanged.

fields.label: Headline
fields.hint: A short name for this beat, e.g. “Act 2 — the firewall”. It is the card's title bar.

fields.label: Beat text
fields.hint: The key content of the beat. The card previews the top ~800 characters and expands into a scrollable panel for the rest.

fields.label: Branch choices
fields.hint: Add a row for each path the story can take. Each gets its own output socket on the card, so you can wire each branch onward while planning.

fields.label: Choice
fields.hint: Short title for this path, e.g. “Go in through the front door”.

fields.label: What happens
fields.hint: One line on where this path leads, so a branching beat reads at a glance.

fields.label: Width (px)
fields.hint: How wide the card is on the canvas, in pixels.

fields.label: Card colour
fields.hint: Pick any colour. Colour-coding by act, character or branch is usually the clearest.
